system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker HOT_G02345 (hotspot mutation in gene G02345).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking: The result looks consistent across lineages, and target expression is similar between the altered and other lines, so this doesn't seem driven by expression. The mutant lines depend on G02345 for their own survival, but the other lines average -0.41 and G02345 isn't flagged as broadly essential, which leaves room for a selective window. I'll register this and replicate it.

Effect is independent of target expression level and holds across breast, endometrial, bladder, ovarian, and gastric lineages.

findings.claim: Cancer lines with a HOT_G02345 hotspot mutation depend on G02345 itself more than other lines (lineage-adjusted beta -0.54 in discovery; replicated in held-out Broad, beta -0.41, p=4e-13, and independent Sanger, beta -0.59, p=6e-12). Effect is not explained by target expression or a single lineage (seen in breast, endometrial, bladder, ovarian, gastric, and others), and G02345 is not broadly essential, so a selective window appears to exist. Consistent with mutant-driven oncogene addiction; the mechanism needs direct validation.

input.summary: Best candidate: G02345, the gene carrying the HOT_G02345 hotspot. Lines with the hotspot are more dependent on G02345 than other lines (discovery: 51/62 altered lines strongly dependent vs 180/564 others; lineage-adjusted effect t=-13). The association is not driven by one lineage, is not an expression artifact, and was replicated in both held-out Broad lines and independent Sanger screens (one-sided p < 1e-11 in each). Caveats: the dependency is a self-dependency on the mutated gene, so the data cannot separate a neomorphic mutant dependence from simple loss of the gene; non-mutant lines still show moderate dependence (mean -0.41), so the therapeutic window is real but not absolute. Only one hypothesis was registered and tested; the other alternative biomarker-target pairs in the scan (e.g., MUT_G15196 and LOSS_G02315 with G02345) were weaker and were not pursued.
